---
order: 2
unit: values
title: The world behind the source
node: AC9HH7S06 n2
summary: "A source is also a window on the society that made it. Read it for the attitudes and values it shows: in its words, in its pictures and symbols, and in what it takes for granted. Describe what a past value was and how the source shows it before judging it by today's standards."
language: maths
hook: "A saying of Confucius, studied for centuries, says women and servants are hard to handle. What does that tell us about the world it came from?"
---
A source can tell you about more than its maker. It can show the **attitudes and values** of their whole society: what people thought was right, important or normal. Historians call this reading **the world behind the source**.

Values show up in three places:

- **the words** a source uses,
- **the pictures and symbols** it uses,
- **what it takes for granted**: things it doesn't bother to explain, because everyone then accepted them.

**Confucius** (551 to 479 BCE) was a teacher. After he died, his followers collected his sayings in a book, the *Analects*, and officials in Han China studied it closely. One saying, in the words the Australian Curriculum uses, is:

> "Women and underlings are especially difficult to handle."

*Underlings* means servants and people of low rank. We are reading this saying as evidence of past attitudes, not because it is right.

## Predict: what can it show?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing first shows whether students stop at judging the saying or go on to ask what it shows about the society."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "What can a saying like this tell a historian?"
  options:
    - "What some people at the time thought about who should be in charge"
    - "Nothing, because it is unfair by today's standards"
    - "Probably how most women and servants really behaved at home"
    - "What Confucius thought, and nothing about anyone else then"
  actual: "It shows attitudes of the time about rank and who should manage whom. It was collected, taught and studied for centuries, so it tells us about more than one man. Today we can also say it is unfair; both can be true."
```

## Try: which attitude?

```step
stage: run
insight: "Naming the attitude in plain words is the first move in reading the world behind the source."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Which attitude does the saying show?"
  options:
    - "Women and servants were seen as people for men in charge to manage"
    - "Women and servants were seen as in charge of the household"
    - "Everyone in the household was seen as equal"
    - "Confucius was seen as a difficult person to manage"
  answer: 0
  feedback:
    - null
    - "'Difficult to handle' means someone else is doing the handling. Who?"
    - "The saying sorts people into those who handle and those who are handled."
    - "Read it again: who does he say is difficult?"
  explain: "The saying takes for granted a household where men of rank are in charge and others are managed."
```

Was your guess right? A saying can show a value without ever stating it.

## Worked example: words, pictures, what it takes for granted

| Where to look | In the Confucius saying |
|---|---|
| The words | "Handle": women and servants are to be managed |
| Who is speaking, to whom | A respected teacher, to male students |
| What it takes for granted | A household where a man is in charge and everyone has a rank |
| So the value it shows | Order by rank, with men of rank at the top |

Pictures work the same way. In 1972, archaeologists opened a Han tomb at **Mawangdui**, in Changsha. It held a T-shaped painting on silk, about 2 metres long, made about 2,200 years ago for a noblewoman, Lady Xin Zhui. From top to bottom it shows:

- **Heaven**: the sun (with a crow in it) and the moon (with a toad and a hare)
- **The lady**: with attendants around her; below, her family make offerings for her
- **The world below**: strange creatures that were believed to guard the body

You can see the painting on the [Hunan Museum's page](https://web.hnmuseum.com/en/node/7370).

Nib's notes below, and Mei later in the lesson, are made up for this lesson.

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Finding where Nib's judgement stops the inquiry names the slip; the banner check moves the same reading to a picture."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "values.txt#nib"
      text: "Click the first line where Nib's thinking goes wrong."
      answer: 3
      fault: logic
      misconception: judge-only-by-today
      explain: "Line 3: Nib's judgement in line 2 is fine, but it is not the end of the job. The saying is good evidence of attitudes to rank and gender at the time, which is what a historian is asking about."
    hint: ["Judging a source as unfair is fine. Is that where a historian's job ends?", "Can a source you disagree with still tell you something about its time?"]
    smaller:
      check:
        type: question
        q: "A 100-year-old school rule says 'Girls may not study science.' What can it tell a historian?"
        options:
          - "What the school thought girls should learn back then"
          - "Nothing, because the rule is unfair"
          - "That girls back then had no interest in science"
          - "That the rule is still a good idea today"
        answer: 0
        feedback:
          - null
          - "It is unfair. It is also evidence of what people then believed."
          - "A rule shows what adults decided, not what girls wanted."
          - "Using it as evidence doesn't mean agreeing with it."
        explain: "A rule you disagree with is still good evidence of the values of the time."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "In the middle of the Mawangdui painting, the lady has attendants and her family make offerings for her. Which values does that show?"
      options:
        - "Her high rank mattered even after death, and family had a duty to the dead"
        - "Han people did not care about what happened after someone died"
        - "Every person in Han China was buried with a painting like this one"
        - "Servants and noblewomen were treated as equals in Han China"
      answer: 0
      feedback:
        - null
        - "A painting this carefully made, put in a tomb, shows they cared a great deal."
        - "This was a noblewoman's tomb. Most people could not afford anything like it."
        - "Attendants around her show rank, not equality."
      explain: "The picture takes for granted that rank and family duty carry on after death."
```

### Find Nib's mistake

### The silk painting

## Vary: one source, everyone?

```step
stage: modify
insight: "The opposite slip, one source standing for a whole society, checks that students keep a value to the people who held it."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Mei says: 'Confucius said it, so every person in Han China believed women and servants were hard to handle.' What is the best reply?"
  options:
    - "It shows a view taught to officials, not what everyone believed"
    - "That is right, because Confucius was the most famous teacher"
    - "No, because Confucius lived before the Han, so it tells us nothing"
    - "No, because sayings never show what a society valued"
  answer: 0
  feedback:
    - null
    - "Being famous and studied makes it important, not shared by everyone."
    - "Han officials studied the Analects closely, so it does tell us about Han values."
    - "Sayings can show values. The question is whose."
  explain: "A source shows values held by some people at the time. How widely they were held needs more evidence."
```

## Practise: what each part shows

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Matching each part of the painting to a value checks the picture-reading move on its own."
check:
  type: match
  q: "Match each part of the Mawangdui painting to the attitude or value it suggests."
  pairs:
    - ["Family members making offerings", "A duty to care for the dead"]
    - ["Attendants around the lady", "Rank still mattered after death"]
    - ["Heaven at the top, with the sun and moon", "Belief in a world beyond this one"]
    - ["Creatures guarding the world below", "Care to keep the dead person's body safe"]
  explain: "Each part shows something the painters and the family took for granted."
```

## Make: values behind a source, in your book

```step
stage: make
insight: "Writing an attitude and how the source shows it, before judging it, is the checkpoint in their own words."
check: { type: reflect, text: "In my own book I chose a source from the society our class is studying (or one in this lesson), wrote one attitude or value it shows and how it shows it (words, picture or what it takes for granted), and then, separately, what I think of that value today. A partner read it and gave feedback." }
```

Write it in your own book or document, not on this page. Your partner or teacher reads it.

## Typical: a face on a coin

Roman coins usually carried the emperor's head and his titles. Everyone who paid for bread held one.

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "A coin shows values through a symbol in another society, and makes 'what it takes for granted' concrete."
check:
  type: question
  q: "What does putting the emperor's head on everyday coins suggest about Roman values?"
  options:
    - "Rulers wanted everyone, every day, to know who was in charge"
    - "Romans thought coins had to show a person to be worth money"
    - "Every Roman agreed the emperor was a good ruler"
    - "Coins were made only for the emperor's own use"
  answer: 0
  feedback:
    - null
    - "Coins could show other things too. Why choose the ruler?"
    - "A coin shows what the ruler wanted people to see, not what they all thought."
    - "Ordinary people used them every day; that's the point."
  explain: "Symbols on everyday things show what a society's rulers wanted taken for granted."
```

## Wider: judging the past

```step
stage: make
tier: wider
insight: "Weighing empathy against critique is where historians balance describing a past value with judging it."
check:
  type: question
  q: "A historian studies the Confucius saying. Which approach is best?"
  options:
    - "Describe the attitude in its own time first, then judge it"
    - "Judge it by today's standards, since that is what matters now"
    - "Never judge the past, because people then knew no better"
    - "Change the words so the saying sounds fair today"
  answer: 0
  feedback:
    - null
    - "That tells us about us. What about them?"
    - "Historians can judge; they describe first, so the judgement is fair to the evidence."
    - "Changing a source destroys the evidence."
  explain: "Describe first, in its own time, then judge, so the judgement rests on an accurate picture."
```

Typical and wider steps are extras on the same idea. You do not need them to finish the lesson.

```teacher
learning: identify attitudes and values of the past in a source, and explain how
  its words, pictures or assumptions show them, before judging them
summary: Identify the attitudes and values of the society that produced a
  source, explain how the source shows them (words, images and symbols, what it
  takes for granted), and try to understand them in their time rather than only
  by today's standards.
time: 40
timing: Predict and Try 7 min · Worked example 13 min · Vary 5 min · Practise 5
  min · Make 10 min. Typical and wider steps are extras and not counted in this.
goals:
  - I can name an attitude or value a source shows.
  - I can explain how the source shows it, using its words, a picture or what it
    takes for granted.
  - I can describe a past value in its time before I judge it.
struggle: Students either refuse to engage ('it's sexist, so it's useless') or
  treat one source as everyone's view. Both are fair starting points; the lesson
  asks for the next step.
before: >-
  AC9HH7S06 n2. Builds on n1 (perspective is not content).


  **The Confucius saying.** ACARA's elaboration quotes it, so the lesson uses
  ACARA's wording (Analects 17.25) and introduces it as a perspective to
  analyse, not as true (rules T8, T20: include, don't avoid). Translations
  differ: the word often translated "women" may mean women of the household or
  concubines, and "underlings" small or low people; scholars disagree about how
  widely it was meant. Students may react strongly. That is a fair response: the
  lesson keeps the judgement and adds the historian's question (what does it
  show about the society?). Don't ask students about their own families or
  beliefs. People and power (`people-7/womens-roles`) has the evidence about
  women's lives in Han China; this lesson doesn't repeat it.


  **The Mawangdui painting** (checked 1 Nov 2026, Hunan Museum): T-shaped silk
  painting from Tomb 1, Mawangdui, Changsha, found in 1972, Western Han, about
  205 cm long; heaven with the sun crow and the moon toad and hare; the lady
  with attendants and her family making offerings; creatures believed to guard
  the body. Students read it in words; the link goes to the museum's page. This
  lesson shows no human remains (the preserved body in the same tomb is not
  mentioned to students; see Beliefs and practices if your class uses it).


  Typical: Roman coins with the emperor's head and titles (standard; not
  rechecked).


  Usually Year 7; not yet tried with a class. No board or clips.


  Relevant ACARA AC9HH7S06 elaborations (examples, not a checklist):
  "identifying perspectives in a historical source, such as the saying of
  Confucius, 'Women and underlings are especially difficult to handle', and
  discussing the values and attitudes of the society that produced it";
  "identifying the possible meanings of, and attitudes and values shown by,
  images and symbols in primary sources, such as funerary texts or religious
  manuscripts".


  First Nations: the node's typical width mentions sources from the Deep Time
  unit; this lesson uses none (rules T1). Teach that part with First Nations-led
  resources.
running:
  - "Predict: let students say what they think of the saying first; then ask
    what it shows about the past."
  - "Try: ask who is doing the 'handling'."
  - "Worked example: cover the 'So the value it shows' row and let pairs write
    it."
  - "Vary: ask who studied the Analects (officials), and who we don't hear from."
  - "Make: students write in their own book; a partner checks that the
    description comes before the judgement."
stuck:
  - see: A student says the saying is wrong, so it's useless.
    ask: You're right that it's unfair. What does it tell us people believed then?
    fix: Judging is allowed; describe what it shows first.
  - see: A student says everyone in Han China thought this.
    ask: Who studied this book? Whose views don't we have?
    fix: It shows a view taught to officials; others need more evidence.
  - see: A student describes what the painting shows but not the value.
    ask: Why would someone put that in a tomb? What did they care about?
    fix: "Name the value: rank, family duty, belief in an afterlife."
support: Give the three places to look (words, pictures, what it takes for
  granted) as a card, with one example each.
stretch: Some readers today argue the saying meant only some women of the
  household. How would a historian decide between readings?
leads: Continue to Missing voices.
exit:
  q: Name one value shown by the Confucius saying or the Mawangdui painting, and
    say how the source shows it.
  a: "For example: order by rank, with men of rank in charge (the saying says
    women and servants are to be 'handled'); duty to the dead (the painting
    shows the family making offerings)."
explain: Sources show the attitudes and values of their society in their words,
  pictures and what they take for granted. Describe the value in its own time
  first; then you can judge it.
sources:
  - title: T-shaped painting on silk, Mawangdui Tomb 1 (Hunan Museum)
    url: https://web.hnmuseum.com/en/node/7370
    checked: 2026-11-01
  - title: "Confucius (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy): dates and the Analects"
    url: https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2005/entries/confucius/
    checked: 2026-11-01
class:
  inquiry:
    q: If historians in 2,000 years found only our school's rules, what would they
      decide we valued?
    prompts:
      - Which rules would they misread?
      - What would the rules take for granted?
    notes: Use the school's published rules, not anything about individual students.
  activities:
    - at: investigate
      kind: discussion
      title: Read the painting
      minutes: 5
      do: >
        Show the museum's picture of the Mawangdui painting. Pairs pick one part
        and say what it shows, then what value it suggests.
      notes: Keep description and value separate. Don't show images of the preserved
        body from the same tomb.
  questions:
    - at: make
      title: Check before moving on
      type: question
      q: A source shows a value you think is unfair today. What should a historian do?
      options:
        - Describe what it shows about its time, then judge it
        - Leave the source out, so the unfair view isn't spread
        - Change its words a little so it sounds fairer today
      answer: 0
      explain: Describe first, then judge; the source stays as evidence.
      feedback:
        - null
        - Leaving it out hides evidence of the past.
        - Changing a source destroys the evidence.
```
